topic: making wooden clogs: alder soles, hollowing the seat, lasting the leather upper and nailing irons

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-6)
provenance.notes: pisane niezaleznie, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: wilgotnosciomierz do blokow olchowych

base: I have started making my own clogs and the soles keep splitting along the grain as they dry.
A beech last came with the bench and it is the only shape I have to work over.
A moisture meter lives in the drawer and I press it into every block before I cut.
I felled the alder in March and roughed out four soles the same week with the stock knife.
Should the block be seasoned before roughing out, or is green wood the right thing for a sole?
Green wood is right for roughing, since alder cuts like cheese when wet and like stone when dry.
The splitting comes afterwards, from drying the roughed soles too fast in a warm room.
Stack them loose under cover where the air moves freely but the sun never reaches them.
Three months of slow drying will lose you nothing, while three weeks of quick drying loses half.
I stacked the next batch loose in the open shed and they have dried without a single split.
The moisture meter reads about eighteen per cent now, down from thirty when I cut them.
The hollowing is giving me trouble because the seat comes out deeper on one side than the other.
Is that the fault of the knife, or of the way I hold the sole against the bench?
It is the hold, since a sole that rocks on the bench takes the knife unevenly at every stroke.
Wedge the toe hard against the stop and keep your knee across the waist of the sole.
Work the hollower from both sides toward the middle and never in one long sweep.
Check the seat with your palm rather than your eye, because the hand feels a hollow the eye misses.
Wedging the toe cured it and the seats now come out even on both sides of the sole.
I have four soles ready and would like to cut the uppers from a shoulder of leather.
The beech last is a size too large for the foot I am making these clogs for.
I could pad the last with felt, or I could cut the upper smaller and stretch it on.
Which of the two is less likely to leave me with a crooked seam at the heel?
Pad the last, because leather cut short pulls the seam round toward the outside of the heel.
Felt glued to the last holds its shape and can be taken off again for the next pair.
Cut the upper with the backbone of the hide running from toe to heel, and never across.
Leather cut across the back will stretch sideways and the clog grows wide within a month.
Wet the upper before you last it, and leave it on the last until it is bone dry.
I padded the last with felt and the upper came off it with a straight seam at last.
Nailing the upper to the sole is slow and two nails have split out through the edge.
I am using ordinary tacks because the proper clog nails were nowhere to be had.
Does the nail really matter that much, or should I simply set them further in?
The nail matters a great deal, since a clog nail has a flat blade that cuts across the grain.
A round tack acts as a wedge instead and splits the sole exactly as you have found.
Set them a good quarter inch in from the edge and drive with a light, quick blow.
If you cannot find clog nails, farriers will sometimes keep something close enough to serve.
I found proper clog nails at a farrier and nailed a whole pair without splitting anything.
The clogs have been worn daily for a month and the soles are wearing at the toe.
My grandfather had irons on his, though I have no idea at all how they were fitted.
Are irons worth putting on, or would a rubber strip do the same work more quietly?
Irons are worth it on stone and cobble, where rubber wears away in a matter of weeks.
They are nailed cold through the same holes each time they are renewed, so drill once and well.
Rubber is quieter and kinder indoors, but it grips badly on wet flags and worn steps.
Many people iron the heel and rubber the toe, which answers both wants at once.
